text: Luca Ricci Turns Optical Distortion into Atmospheric Furniture Menu Luca Ricci Turns Optical Distortion into Atmospheric Furniture Words by Eric David 21 July 2026 Beautiful Things Location Milan, Italy Luca Ricci Turns Optical Distortion into Atmospheric Furniture Words by Eric David 21 July 2026 Beautiful Things Milan, Italy Milan, Italy Location Milan-based designer Luca Ricci works fluently across art direction, branding and graphic design, bringing to each discipline the same experimental fervour and attention to detail. His recent foray into furniture design translates this background into two custom-designed pieces informed as much by questions of functionality as by the instincts of someone attuned to image-making. Plissè Block , a sofa for Milanese menswear label Fivefourfive , and Flower Block , a DJ console built for Shablo and his collaborators at the Sanremo Music Festival, were created for very different contexts, yet share a precise visual language that combines clean, rectilinear volumes with fluted, translucent surfaces, using optical distortion to turn functional objects into atmospheric devices. Flower Block render © Luca Ricci. Plissé Block at FiveFourFive 's Milan store.  Photography by Nicolò Panzeri. Flower Block at the Teatro Arcimboldi, Milan, during  a performance by Shablo in November 2025. Commissioned for the opening of Fivefourfive’s flagship store in Milan’s Brera district, designed by Studio Musa , Plissè Block was conceived as the space’s centrepiece. Ricci found his starting point in a historical sketch by Le Corbusier , borrowing the proportions of the architect’s LC2 sofa and stripping the reference back to a set of formal ratios before rebuilding it through an entirely different material logic. Composed of three modules, two side blocks and a central element, and set on hidden castors, the sofa’s structure is made entirely of glass: an inner smooth layer provides support, while an outer fluted layer wraps the volume in a pleated optical skin. Like pleated fabric, from which the piece takes its name, the fluted surface creates a sense of repetition, movement and controlled tension. As light passes through it, it bends, fragments and softens what lies behind, making the object appear to shift according to viewpoint and illumination. The effect is sharpened by the contrast with six red velvet cushions: three rectangular seats and three cylindrical backrests. Against the cool precision of glass, the red velvet introduces warmth, tactility and an unmistakable note of theatricality, while further accentuating the design’s graphic sensibility. Plissé Block at FiveFourFive 's Milan store.  Photography by Nicolò Panzeri. Plissé Block at FiveFourFive 's Milan store.  Photography by Nicolò Panzeri. Plissé Block render © Luca Ricci. Photography by Nicolò Panzeri. Plissé Block render © Luca Ricci. Plissé Block render © Luca Ricci. Plissé Block render © Luca Ricci. Plissé Block render © Luca Ricci. Plissé Block render © Luca Ricci. Flower Block render © Luca Ricci. Theatricality also defines Flower Block, and for good reason: the DJ console was designed for Shablo , Guè , Joshua and Tormento 's joint performance at the 2025 Sanremo Music Festival. Built from transparent fluted plexiglass rather than glass, it consists of two volumes, a long horizontal block and a vertical support column, both hollowed out to accommodate floral arrangements. The choice of flowers is not arbitrary. Best known for its music festival, Sanremo has also been hosting an annual flower festival for more than a century, cementing its reputation as the "Città dei Fiori", or City of Flowers . Placed inside the console, the flowers appear blurred, multiplied and abstracted by the ribbed surfaces, transforming it into a mesmerising floral tableau. Here, too, functionality is carefully absorbed into the design. Hidden wheels allow the console to move without interrupting its clean silhouette, a raised perimeter ledge conceals cables from the DJ equipment, and rear access panels allow the flowers to be easily arranged and replaced. Flower Block render © Luca Ricci. Flower Block at the Teatro Arcimboldi, Milan, during  a performance by Shablo in November 2025. Flower Block render © Luca Ricci. Flower Block render © Luca Ricci. Seen together, the two works suggest how Ricci's graphic sensibility informs his furniture design. Minimal in form yet visually seductive, both pieces are functional objects that double as scenographic presences, using material properties like transparency and texture to shape how each object is perceived . In this sense, Ricci's foray into furniture reads as an extension of his previous practice rather than a departure from it: a translation of the same instinct for image-making into objects built to be used as much as seen. Bench Hand Painted Glass W 173 D 42 H 42 2023 Limited Edition 8 + 4AP LV Collection Within our studio, material research is very often the starting point of a project, allowing form to emerge from hands on experimentation rather than predetermined blueprints. For the LV Collection, we have focused exclusively on glass, exploring its limits through the reinterpretation of Lustro Veneziano; an ancient, disappearing artisanal technique. Historically confined to small scale decorative objects, Lustro involves applying a thin film of metallic oxides to glass, which fires into a light refracting, iridescent finish. We reintroduced this heritage craft into a contemporary context by expanding its scale, applying it to large design pieces for the very first time. By layering and overlapping hand painted glass sheets, the objects form dynamic optical compositions that shift with light and perspective. More than mere design objects, these pieces function as physical archives of a human legacy. The rigorous, slow-paced collaboration with master artisans is central to the work’s significance; a process where the intuition of the human hand achieves nuances that no automated machinery can replicate. By scaling up this meticulous method, the collection actively resists the erasure of historical craftsmanship. It serves as a vital case study in heritage preservation, proving that endangered traditions can be reactivated not just as nods to the past, but as raw, living material for the future of contemporary design. Side Table Resin W 45 D 45 H 45 2019 Limited Edition 8 + 4AP ph: Mathijs Labadie Available exclusively in the Americas/Europe through Studiotwentyseven The G Collection is a series of sculptural resin furniture defined by geometric clarity and a meticulous production process. The collection draws inspiration from the architectural lineage of Carlo Scarpa’s interplay of positive and negative volumes, as well as Frank Lloyd Wright’s early geometric structures, such as the 1939 Taliesin West. The foundational piece, the GSD Console, established the collection's signature language: pure lines, precise 90-degree angles, and thin, structural profiles. While resin is synthetic, its interaction with light gives it an organic quality. The material allows for exceptionally sharp edges that refract and reflect their environment. Depending on the lighting, a single piece can shift dramatically from a deep, dense shadow to a vibrant, translucent luminosity. This visual volatility is paired with a distinct tactile contrast; the polished surfaces are clinically smooth yet surprisingly warm to the touch. Each piece is handmade by skilled artisans in the Netherlands. The complex, time-consuming casting and polishing processes require absolute precision to maintain the structural integrity of the sharp angles, elevating these functional forms into works of collectible design. Low Table Hand Painted Glass W 170 D 35 H 85 2024 Limited Edition 8 + 4AP Available exclusively through Collectional LV Collection Within our studio, material research is very often the starting point of a project, allowing form to emerge from hands on experimentation rather than predetermined blueprints. For the LV Collection, we have focused exclusively on glass, exploring its limits through the reinterpretation of Lustro Veneziano; an ancient, disappearing artisanal technique. Historically confined to small scale decorative objects, Lustro involves applying a thin film of metallic oxides to glass, which fires into a light refracting, iridescent finish. We reintroduced this heritage craft into a contemporary context by expanding its scale, applying it to large objects for the very first time. By layering and overlapping hand painted glass sheets , dynamic optical compositions are formed, that shift with light and perspective. More than mere design objects, these pieces function as physical archives of a human legacy. The true value of the work resides in the rigorous, slow paced collaboration with master artisans; a process where the intuition of the human hand achieves nuances that no automated machinery can replicate. By scaling up this meticulous method, the collection actively resists the erasure of historical craftsmanship. It serves as a vital case study in heritage preservation, proving that endangered traditions can be reactivated not just as nods to the past, but as raw, living material for the future of contemporary design.
